connection: Session 26 established awaited repository/service flow. Those methods do not yet accept or observe cancellation. Propagate cancellation through the real asynchronous repository and service workflow.
objectives: Fix the real CS4014 bug: add await to Program.cs's clockEntryService.Clockout(1) call and remove the pragma suppression, confirming the build is warning-free without it.
Explain why the fix changes CalculateTotalHours's printed total from a near-zero accident to a real, deterministic, non-trivial number of hours.

Read IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry's CancellationToken cancellationToken = default parameter and confirm, by reading ClockEntryRepository's real implementation, that it is never actually checked or passed anywhere.
Contrast that decorative token with CancellableEntrySource, a new extension whose CancellationToken is genuinely passed to Task.Delay and can actually cancel an in-flight operation.

visuals.title: Before the fix: a race with an accidental near-correct answer
visuals.explanation: clockEntryService.Clockout(1) without await lets Program.cs call CalculateTotalHours before Clockout's body has necessarily finished -- the near-zero total was luck, not correctness.

visuals.title: After the fix: ClockIn, then Clockout, then the total, guaranteed in order
visuals.explanation: await clockEntryService.Clockout(1); ensures Clockout's entire body -- including SaveClockEntry -- completes before CalculateTotalHours runs.

visuals.title: A CancellationToken parameter is not automatically functional
visuals.explanation: IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry accepts a CancellationToken but its real implementation never reads it -- passing one has no effect on the real GetClockEntry today.

visuals.title: CancellableEntrySource shows what a real, functioning token looks like
visuals.explanation: await Task.Delay(latency, cancellationToken) genuinely observes cancellation -- a real contrast to GetClockEntry's decorative parameter.

preQuiz.prompt: Why did Program.cs's unawaited Clockout(1) call produce a near-zero total-hours output rather than a clearly wrong one?
options: ClockIn and the fire-and-forget Clockout run essentially back-to-back with almost no real elapsed time between them, and if CalculateTotalHours runs before Clockout's SaveClockEntry completes, GetEmployeeClockEntries may find zero completed entries in the requested window -- a near-zero result was the accidental, not guaranteed, outcome
The total was always correct -- there was never a real bug
CalculateTotalHours has a rounding bug unrelated to await
preQuiz.explanation: This is the real, documented consequence of the CS4014 warning -- Session 26 identified it; this session fixes it and explains exactly why the output changes.

preQuiz.prompt: After adding await to clockEntryService.Clockout(1), what does Program.cs now guarantee about the order of operations?
options: ClockIn completes, then Clockout's entire body (including the real SaveClockEntry call inside it) completes, THEN CalculateTotalHours runs -- removing the race entirely
Nothing changes -- await has no effect on execution order here
ClockIn and Clockout now run concurrently instead of the reverse
preQuiz.explanation: await is precisely what removes the race: the calling code cannot proceed past the awaited call until it has genuinely finished.

preQuiz.prompt: Does passing a real, non-default CancellationToken to the current GetClockEntry implementation actually let you cancel an in-flight lookup?
options: No -- the real ClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry implementation never reads or checks its cancellationToken parameter anywhere in its body; passing one has no observable effect today
Yes -- every async method automatically respects any CancellationToken passed to it
Only if the lookup takes longer than one second
preQuiz.explanation: This is confirmed by reading the production code directly -- the parameter exists in the signature (the only CancellationToken in the whole codebase) but is unused, decorative.

concept.title: Cancellation is a cooperative request
paragraphs: A CancellationToken carries a request to stop. Code at a cancellable boundary must observe it; adding a parameter without using or forwarding it changes nothing.
Cancellation is not failure and should not be converted into an unrelated domain exception.

concept.title: Propagate the same token
paragraphs: App passes the token to the service, and the service passes it to the repository. Each layer should avoid replacing it with CancellationToken.None.
The operation that waits on I/O is usually where cancellation becomes effective.

concept.title: Test cancellation deterministically
paragraphs: An already-cancelled token gives a deterministic first test. A second test proves normal work still succeeds.
There is no need to preserve a known unawaited-call bug merely to teach cancellation.

lab.objective: Propagate cancellation through the real asynchronous repository and service workflow.
lab.startingCondition: Session 26 established awaited repository/service flow. Those methods do not yet accept or observe cancellation.
steps: Open IClockEntryRepository and locate every asynchronous member introduced in Session 26.
Confirm each asynchronous repository member accepts a CancellationToken parameter named cancellationToken.
Open the repository implementation and pass cancellationToken to any genuinely cancellable operation it performs.
At an in-memory boundary with no naturally cancellable wait, call cancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested before changing or returning state.
Open ClockEntryService and add an optional CancellationToken parameter to each asynchronous public method.
Pass the same cancellationToken to every awaited repository call; do not create a replacement token.
Open PayrollService and add an optional CancellationToken parameter if CalculateTotalHoursAsync awaits repository work.
Pass that same cancellationToken through the awaited repository call.
Open Program.cs and create or reuse one CancellationToken value for the App workflow.
Pass the token from Program.cs through each asynchronous service call.
Create tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/CancellationTests.cs.
In CancellationTests.cs, declare a public sealed class named CancellationTests.
Add a Fact method named RepositoryOperation_WhenTokenAlreadyCancelled_ThrowsOperationCanceledException.
In that test, create a CancellationTokenSource and call Cancel before invoking the repository.
Use Assert.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException> around the cancellable repository operation.
Add a second Fact method named RepositoryOperation_WhenTokenIsActive_CompletesNormally.
In the second test, use CancellationToken.None with the same repository operation.
Assert the normal observable result of that operation.
Run the focused CancellationTests.
Run App and the full solution test suite.
lab.expectedBehavior: Cancellation is meaningful, propagated, and tested rather than decorative.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Keep the lesson synchronized with the cumulative build step.

commit: session-27: teach cancellation and asynchronous exceptions
review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why was it correct for Sessions 5 through 25 to keep Program.cs's Clockout(1) call unawaited, rather than fixing it immediately when it was first introduced?
options: The bug is real, observable, and pedagogically useful exactly as-is -- fixing it only once async/await (Session 26) and cancellation (this session) have been properly taught lets learners understand WHY it's a bug, not just that it is one
It was an oversight that should have been fixed in Session 6
Unawaited async calls are actually correct C# and never need fixing
postQuiz.explanation: This mirrors the production code's own history: the bug exists in production-adjacent code precisely because understanding why it matters requires the async/await knowledge this course builds up to across Sessions 25-27.

postQuiz.prompt: If GetClockEntry's CancellationToken parameter started being genuinely checked (e.g. with cancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()), what real behavior would change for existing callers?
options: Existing callers passing the default token would see no change at all, since a default CancellationToken is never in a cancelled state -- only callers who explicitly pass and trigger a real token would newly observe OperationCanceledException
Every existing call to GetClockEntry would immediately start throwing
The method's return type would need to change
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly why adding real cancellation support to an existing method is usually a safe, additive change -- default(CancellationToken) callers are unaffected.

postQuiz.prompt: What is the real, functional difference in this codebase between a CancellationToken parameter that exists but is unused, and one that is genuinely checked?
options: The unused one (GetClockEntry's) has zero effect on the method's behavior no matter what token is passed; the checked one (CancellableEntrySource's) can genuinely stop the operation early via OperationCanceledException
There is no real difference -- both behave identically
The checked one always runs faster
postQuiz.explanation: This is the entire teaching point of contrasting the two: a CancellationToken parameter's mere presence in a signature proves nothing about whether cancellation actually works.

reflections: Why does fixing Program.cs's real bug in Session 28 (rather than Session 26, where it was first identified) feel like the right pedagogical placement now that you understand cancellation?
Where else in this codebase might a parameter exist in a signature without being genuinely used, the way GetClockEntry's CancellationToken is?
What would you need to change about ClockEntryRepository for GetClockEntry's CancellationToken to become genuinely functional?
whatBreaks: Reverting Program.cs's await fix reintroduces the real race condition between Clockout's completion and CalculateTotalHours's read of GetEmployeeClockEntries, along with the real CS4014 warning that would then need re-suppressing to keep the build warning-free. Assuming GetClockEntry's CancellationToken parameter provides genuine cancellation support (because the parameter exists) would lead to writing cancellation-dependent code around a method that currently cannot honor it.
summary: Program.cs's real, long-standing unawaited Clockout(1) call is fixed here, in the session where async/await and cancellation are both fully in scope: adding await removes the race that made CalculateTotalHours's near-zero output an accident rather than a guarantee, and the CS4014 pragma suppression is removed along with the bug it was protecting. GetClockEntry's CancellationToken parameter is confirmed, by reading its real implementation, to be entirely decorative -- a real contrast to CancellableEntrySource's genuinely functioning one.

extends: cancellation through repository and service boundaries
